title: Turbulent isopycnal mixing dominates thermohaline transformations of intermediate ocean waters

paper_content.abstract: The ocean, because of its ability to store heat and as the biggest mediator of water exchanges on Earth, modulates the climate from years to centuries. By combining Water Mass transformation and the Temporal-Residual-Mean frameworks, together with a direct estimation of turbulent diffusivity (computed through an artificial intelligence method), we determine temperature and salinity transformations along density surfaces. Because isopycnal transformations barely alter the density field, they remain hidden from the ocean dynamics. Here we unveil these hidden, isopycnal transformations from in situ observations at 1000-m depth. We show that these isopycnal transformations are 5 times as large as their diapycnal counterpart and are occurring for ~67% in the Southern Ocean. Our estimations stress the role of the spatially-varying and anisotropic characteristics of isopycnal diffusion, often not considered in ocean models. This has major consequences for our understanding of the role of the ocean in response to anthropogenic climate changes.
paper_content.introduction:
Ocean circulation transports a vast amount of water over the globe (up to 150 Sv, where 1 Sv ≡ 10^6 m^3 s^-1, in the Antarctic Circumpolar Current, for instance)1. This large-scale ocean circulation is also associated with transport of heat (up to 1.5 PW northward at 20°N)2 and freshwater (around 0.5 Sv southward at 35°N in the North Atlantic)3. The former is a fundamental component of the climate equilibrium and adjustment by transporting the excess of heat from the tropics to the poles. Whereas the latter indirectly reflects the geographical pattern of evaporation, precipitation, river discharge, and ice melting, all taking part in the water cycle. In particular, the ocean is the most important region of precipitation and evaporation (i.e., 75% and 85%, respectively), making it particularly relevant for the Earth water cycle4.

Beyond this equilibrated view, the Earth is experiencing changes since the pre-industrial era, with a significant amount of anthropogenically-induced greenhouse gazes released into the atmosphere5. As a consequence, the surface atmospheric temperature is increasing5, despite a significant mitigation by the ocean, with an ocean absorption of about 90% of the Earth’s heat excess5–7. Together with this warming, the water cycle is also affected8. These changes, either directly (when over the ocean) or indirectly through runoffs (when overland), are imprinted in the ocean freshwater transport9,10 through, for instance, modification of the ocean salinity distribution11. Hence, the ocean heat and freshwater transports are central actors of the Earth equilibrium and climate changes.

Mesoscale eddies are ubiquitous worldwide in the ocean12 and, unlike the mean transport, they contribute to the heat and freshwater transport in two-fold. Firstly, equivalently to the laminar component, they move ocean water properties (i.e., its temperature and salinity) in a conserving manner within the ocean. Secondly, eddies also induce a transformation of these properties through turbulent diffusion13 (e.g., mixing cold and warm waters or salty and fresh ones). Transformations of seawater properties can occur either through interactions with the atmosphere at the ocean surface or through turbulent diffusion in the ocean interior. Whereas the former is easier to estimate8,14, the latter has always been more difficult to assess and is often deduced using inverse methodology15–18. Assessing the role of turbulent eddy diffusion for heat and freshwater transports and for the transformation of seawater properties is a timely question of ocean and climate sciences, as demonstrated by numerous numerical model studies19–21.

There has been a large range of studies on Water Mass Transformations22–28. These studies often assess the transformations in terms of temperature and salinity changes, without specifically separating the respective role of isopycnal and diapycnal transformations. In parallel, the role of diapycnal diffusion on temperature and salinity transformations in the ocean interior has been well established16,29. More recently, studies have suggested the key role of isopycnal processes on heat and freshwater uptakes30,31, opening the possibility of an important role of the isopycnal diffusion. This has been further confirmed as potentially important in the North Atlantic for the maintenance of the mean temperature and salinity structure32. However, these studies rely on either numerical models or inverse methods, both intrinsically depending on a chosen closure scheme (and sometimes imposed parameters). Hence, it is key to use direct observations to assess whether isopycnal or diapycnal diffusion is dominant in the ocean interior. Indeed, in ocean science, where reproducible controlled experiments are not possible, the use of direct observations is the only way to validate or invalidate hypotheses derived from these numerical or inverse modeling approaches.

In this work, we use direct observations to assess the changes and transformations of temperature and salinity induced by mesoscale eddy turbulence, which acts as an equivalent isopycnal turbulent diffusion. We show that, at 1000 m depth, these temperature and salinity changes mainly occurred in the Southern Ocean and along the Gulf Stream. These isopycnal changes induce temperature and salinity transformations significantly more important than their diapycnal equivalents. We also conclude that the spatially variable and anisotropic nature of the isopycnal turbulent diffusion is keys for an accurate estimation of the temperature and salinity transformations.
paper_content.results:
The major difficulty of obtaining robust, direct estimations of heat and freshwater transformations by eddies comes from the need of knowing turbulent diffusive coefficients independently of temperature and salinity fields (to avoid the dependence of the results to a closure scheme)33,34. Here, to circumvent this difficulty, we have used the recently estimated diffusivity coefficients35 derived from Argo float deep displacements36. This dataset has been obtained using a class of data-driven Artificial Intelligence methods: the Analog Method37,38. There, the spatially varying and anisotropic diffusivity coefficients were estimated through local tracer dispersion induced by a turbulent velocity field reconstructed from deep Argo displacements. This dataset provides the full diffusivity tensor, explicitly acknowledging the anisotropy, rather than a single diffusivity coefficient, as most commonly done33,34,39. These resulting diffusivity coefficients are strong where the flow is strong (Fig. 1d, e), but with a slight spatial offset with the core of the currents40,41, hence with the largest density gradients. This could be rationalized by the existence of Kinetic Energy transfers42. These coefficients (Fig. 1d, e) together with temperature and salinity fields from gridded ISAS17 product43 (Optimal Interpolation44 from Argo profiles, Fig. 1a, b) allow us to have a direct estimation of isopycnal heat and freshwater transformations and uncover an unobserved facet of deep ocean circulation.

Effect of isopycnal turbulent diffusion
In the present study, we assess the global effect of the turbulent diffusion on temperature and salinity fields. However, because of observational constraints (i.e., the typical parking depth of Argo float deep displacements), our study focuses at 1000 m depth. This depth is particularly relevant for estimating heat and freshwater transports and seawater property transformations for two reasons. (1) It is close to the depth of the maximum of the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (depth of no-motion for this circulation, as estimated at 26.5°N in the North Atlantic by RAPID)45. (2) It is the depth with the largest contrast in salinity46,47, but also includes signatures of the coldest waters47 (Fig. 1).

The transformation of seawater properties works hand in hand with the concept of Water Masses48. Water Masses are volumes of water with consistent seawater properties (Fig. 1f) that are set through ocean-atmosphere exchange at the ocean surface, where water masses originate. They then spread within the ocean through advection and mixing and are transformed by the latter. At 1000 m depth, we will consider three intermediate water masses: Red Sea–Persian Gulf Intermediate Water (RSPGIW) formed in the Red Sea and Persian Gulf49, the Mediterranean Water50 (MW) reaching the Atlantic through the Strait of Gibraltar, and the AntArctic Intermediate Water51 (AAIW) intersecting the 1000-m depth along the Polar Front52. We will also consider more dense Water Masses, namely the North Atlantic Deep Water (NADW), its transformed southern extension, the Circumpolar Deep Water53 (CDW), and the Antarctic Bottom Water54 (AABW). Despite not being their depth of maximum intrusion, these Water Masses are present at 1000 m depth in the high latitudes of the North Atlantic and of the Southern Ocean (Fig. 1f).

To estimate the impact of the turbulent diffusion on the temperature and salinity of these water masses, we follow the Temporal-Residual-Mean framework (see Methods – Isopycnal Turbulent Transformation Framework)13. This framework disentangles advective and mixing effects when eddy turbulence is averaged. This allows for an accurate attribution of eddy-induced transport and transformation. Also, this framework acknowledges that transformations act within isopycnal layers as epineutral flux (Fig. 2). To this purpose averaging are done along-isopycnal, so that fictitious diapycnal transport, due to incorrect estimates of the isopycnal slopes, can be limited55. This transformation-induced process has almost no signature on the density field (except for the weak cabbeling and thermobaricity components, although they remain crucial for the density transformations56), nor pressure, nor circulation. As a consequence, there is no impact on Potential Energy, and it can act passively, as long as Eddy Kinetic Energy remains to maintain the turbulent diffusion. In this sense, for the ocean dynamics, it remains hidden along the isopycnals (Fig. 1c). However, it still contributes to heat and freshwater transports from cold to warm and from salty to fresh regions, respectively. This process can be described in the form of temperature and salinity rates of change or of water-mass transformation rates (see Methods – Water Mass Transformation Rates). The rates of change of a material property (temperature or salinity) measure the amount of warming/cooling or salinification/freshening induced by the isopycnal turbulent diffusion; whereas the transformation accounts for the amount of seawater that have their properties transformed by this process.

Rates of temperature and salinity change
As mentioned above, the isopycnal diffusion of temperature and salinity can be assessed as the induced rates of change in terms of temperature and salinity [see Methods – (10)]. High magnitudes of the rates of change are due to high diffusivity coefficients, sharp isopycnal temperature or salinity gradients, or a combination of both. At 1000 m depth, we find that they are of the order of kelvins per year or tenth of (g kg^-1) per year [or a few 10^-8 K s^-1 and 10^-9 g kg^-1 s^-1] for temperature and salinity, respectively. These rates of change are mainly located in the Southern Ocean, along the Antarctic Circumpolar Current, and, to a lesser extent, in the North West of the North Atlantic (Figs. 3a and 4a). Indeed, the Southern Ocean accounts for 67% of the global rates of change for temperature and salinity [as measured by the R^2 of the transformations described in (11)], despite representing only 31% of the global ocean area. When including the North Atlantic it reaches 95% for temperature and salinity rates of change. A local maximum of these rates of change can be seen in the Zapiola gyre, which corresponds to a local maximum of diffusivity coefficients (Fig. 1d, e). There is also significant rates of change along the Agulhas return current and its merging with the Antarctic Circumpolar Current, which also corresponds to a local maximum of diffusivity coefficients. Indeed, between South Africa and the Kerguelen plateau, there is a warming and salinification of the relatively cold and salty AAIW (Figs. 3a and 4a), a cooling and freshening of the relatively warm and fresh AAIW, and a warming and salinification of the warm and salty residual of RSGPIW (trapped in the Agulhas system57, Fig. 1b).

Unlike the geographical map that reveals where the rates of change are located, the TS-diagram (i.e., representation with temperature-salinity axes) reveals which water masses are subjected to the isopycnal diffusion (i.e., change along isopycnals). This can be represented globally (insets in Figs. 3a and 4a) or displayed for each relevant basin (following the division of Fig. 1f), which allows a simpler relation with local Water Masses (Fig. 3b–e and 4b–e). In the North Atlantic, despite the weak isopycnal turbulent diffusion coefficients in the subtropical gyre interior (Fig. 1d, e), temperature and salinity rates of change within the MW (along the 27.6-27.8 kg m^-3 density class) are visible with a slight cooling and a freshening of MW (Fig. 3b). A more important cooling and freshening is also visible at the edge between MW and NADW. In the Southern Ocean, the geographical separation is quite revealing. It suggests different water masses at play for each of the three sectors (Atlantic, Indian, and Pacific). In the Atlantic sector of the Southern Ocean, we observe a cooling and freshening of CDW and a warming and salinification of AAIW and AABW (Figs. 3c and 4c). In the Indian and Pacific sectors, the rates of change correspond to a warming and salinification of the AABW, a cooling and freshening of the CDW, a warming and salinification of the coldest and freshest portion of the AAIW, and a cooling and freshening of the warmest and saltiest portion of the AAIW (Figs. 3d, e and 4d, e). In the Indian sector, there is also a warming and salinification of the warmer portion of the AAIW, which derives from RSPGIW57.

Water mass transformations
To further quantify these effects, the isopycnal turbulent diffusion can also be expressed as Water Masses Transformation (see Methods – Water Mass Transformation Rates). As discussed earlier, since the isopycnal temperature and salinity gradients are important given the range of different Water Masses. At 25°W we have: AntArctic Bottom Water (AABW), AntArctic Intermediate Water (AAIW), Mediterranean Water (MW), North Atlantic Deep Water (NADW), and Circumpolar Deep Water (CDW). As suggested by the schematic (a and b), it is possible to compute the rates of change, following (10), and the corresponding water mass transformation, following (11), associated to a tracer (e.g., temperature or salinity).

To compare the isopycnal and diapycnal transformations, we measure their amplitude through their standard deviation along the density coordinate. We find that the temperature and salinity isopycnal transformations are 3 and 5 times as large as the diapycnal ones (colored-bars vs cyan line in Fig. 5a, c), respectively. Note that this result contrasts with density transformations for which, as expected, diapycnal transformations is the dominant factor over isopycnal ones, except for a few specific Water Masses (i.e., Subantarctic Mode Water, AAIW, and CDW), for which cabbeling and thermobaricity are important factors56.

These dominant isopycnal transformations reveal a mean density gain and loss of +1.5 Sv and -1.9 Sv, respectively. The density transformations correspond to three regimes in density coordinates (Fig. 5): a warming and salinification of the lightest water, a cooling and freshening of density classes between 27.35 and 28 kg m^-3, and a warming and salinification of the densest water. As expected within an isopycnal framework, transformations with respect to neutral density classes show that density gain and loss by cooling and warming are associated to density loss and gain by freshening and salinification, respectively, preserving the density field (Fig. 5e). Looking at water classes and regional separation, we find warming and salinification of the lightest class of AAIW and cooling of the densest class of AAIW. This mainly occurs in the Indian sector of the Southern Ocean. On the other hand, transformations associated with CDW and AABW exhibit a warming and salinification, which mainly occurred in the Atlantic sector of the Southern Ocean, and to a second degree in the Pacific sector for CDW. A transformation peak is also visible in the North Atlantic sector. It corresponds to a cooling compensated by a freshening at the edge between MW and NADW. Similarly, in the same sector, the full range of MW is also transformed through cooling and freshening, whereas a slight warming and salinification also occur for the NADW.

To better understand the role and to assess the importance of spatially varying anisotropic diffusivity coefficients36, we have tested a range of less complex diffusivity coefficients (see Methods – Alternative Diffusivity Coefficients). To quantitatively test the misestimations of these simplest diffusivity coefficients, we used their relative error in comparison to the most complete version [see Methods – (12)]. The simplest one was a spatially-uniform and isotropic isopycnal diffusivity coefficient (light gray bars in Fig. 5a, b). It mainly preserves the signs of the transformations, but underestimates them by up to 53% for both temperature and salinity. Nonetheless, this approximation warm and salinified AAIW from 27.4 kg m^-3 to 27.5 kg m^-3, whereas it was cool and freshened with the most complete version of the diffusivity. Using spatially-varying and isotropic isopycnal diffusivity coefficients (dark gray bars in Fig. 5a, b) better conserves the shape of the transformations but overestimates by up to 48% both of these temperature and salinity transformations.

Robustness of the isopycnal diffusivity dataset
To test the robustness of our results, we have recomputed the temperature and salinity transformations using two alternative diffusivity coefficient datasets (see Methods – Alternative Diffusivity Coefficients). The first dataset, that we named Groeskamp, estimates diffusivity using salinity observations and assuming the validity of the mixing length theory34. The second dataset, that we named Roach, uses the same deep Argo float displacements than us, but a different methodology: a pairwise dispersion39.

Groeskamp and Roach diffusivities (Fig. 6a, b, respectively) have the same overall pattern as our reference diffusivities (Fig. 1d, e): intensification in western boundary currents and within the Antarctic Circumpolar Current. Because Groeskamp and Roach diffusivity coefficients correspond solely to the cross-flow diffusion, they are more comparable to our secondary diffusivity coefficients (Fig. 1e), which are by construction, weaker than the primary ones. Groeskamp and Roach diffusivity coefficients range between 2000 m^2 s^-1 and 5000 m^2 s^-1 in active regions (as our secondary diffusivity coefficients). In comparison with the two other datasets, Roach diffusivity coefficients are less spatially smooth.

Because the Groeskamp and Roach datasets provide only a single local diffusivity coefficient, we restrict the comparison to the spatially varying and isotropic framework. Computing the temperature and salinity transformations with the different diffusivity coefficient datasets shows the good consistency of the results (Fig. 6c and d). When using our spatially varying and isotropic diffusivity coefficients, we find stronger transformations than those obtained with Groeskamp and Roach diffusivity coefficients. However, the transformations are qualitatively well represented. As expected, the agreement is better when applying the spatially varying and isotropic diffusivity coefficients solely based on the secondary diffusivity coefficients. Here, the agreement is qualitative and quantitative. This stresses the robustness of our described temperature and salinity transformations with respect to the methodology used to infer the diffusivity coefficients.
paper_content.methods:
Isopycnal turbulent transformation framework
Starting from the advection equation for a tracer (which could be temperature or salinity) away from forcing (mainly occurring at the ocean surface) and for high Péclet number (Pe ≫ 1, measuring the advection to diffusion ratio), we have:

D_t C = 0, (1)

where C is the tracer concentration and D_t is the material derivative (=∂_t + u∂_x + v∂_y + w∂_z, where t is time, x, y, and z are the zonal, meridional, and vertical coordinates, and u, v, and w are the zonal, meridional, and vertical velocities).

This equation can be modified to show the evolution of the large-spatial scale or long-timescale by splitting each term in an Eulerian mean (¯) and its associated anomaly ('). This reads:

D_t ¯C = -∂_x ¯(u'C') - ∂_y ¯(v'C') - ∂_z ¯(w'C'), (2)

where D_t is the mean material derivative (=∂_t + ¯u∂_x + ¯v∂_y + ¯w∂_z). This shows that several mean (¯C, ¯u, ¯v, and ¯w) and turbulent (¯(u'C'), ¯(v'C'), and ¯(w'C')) terms contribute to the maintenance of the mean state.

In the Temporal-Residual-Mean framework, we can redistribute the terms13,64 so that the evolution of the mean tracer is:

D_b_t ˆC = d ˆC, (3)

where ˆC is the modified tracer, D_b_t is the modified material derivative [=∂_t + ˆu∂_x + ˆv∂_y + ˆw∂_z, and ˆu=¯u+˜u, ˆv=¯v+˜v, and ˆw=¯w+˜w, where ˜u, ˜v, and ˜w are the zonal, meridional, and vertical eddy-induced velocities, respectively], and d ˆC is the transformation term. This expression suggests that the modified tracer is advected by both the mean and the eddy-induced velocity65 and transformed. In this Temporal-Residual-Mean framework, the eddy-induced advection and the transformation are consequences of the skew-symmetric and symmetric components of the turbulent flux, respectively. This framework is particularly useful to accurately separate and attribute the advection and mixing effects of averaged eddy turbulence. The advection effect only displaces tracer properties, whereas the mixing effect changes tracer properties. Hence, this framework avoids the misinterpretation of eddy-induced transport by horizontal turbulence as a transformation.

In the ocean interior (i.e., below mixed layer depth), we have neglected the potential effect of horizontal transformation (important within the mixed layer). In the rest of the study, we will focus on the isopycnal component of these fluxes and compare it to the diapycnal one. Note that isopycnal heat and freshwater transformations act along a constant density surface, thus, by construction, they avoid density gradients. Although the diapycnal component, induced by small-scale mixing processes66, will be used as a reference. It is worth noting that the use horizontal diffusion instead of isopycnal diffusion outside of the mixed layer is fundamentally flawed55. With this approximation, we would find transformations that are completely missing the correct warming/cooling and freshening/salinification. Also, as expected for such flawed approximation, the compensation between temperature and salinity changes are missed. This would result in unrealistic transformations.

Following a downgradient flux closure13,67 (i.e., Fick’s law), the density-weighted isopycnal transformation reads:

d_i ˆC_so = ∂_z γ ∇_n · K · ∇_n (∂_z γ)^-1, (5)

where ∇_n refers to the gradient along the neutral density (γ) and K is the spatially-varying and anisotropic isopycnal diffusivity tensor. Here, the gradient is computed using the projected nonorthogonal approach68,69. The diffusivity tensor is expressed as:

K = [κ_x~x~ κ_x~y~; κ_x~y~ κ_y~y~], (6)

where x~ and y~ are the zonal and meridional direction along neutral density, respectively, and κ_x~x~, κ_y~y~, and κ_x~y~ are the zonal, meridional, and cross diffusivities along the neutral density, respectively. Hence, the isopycnal transformations for a spatially varying and anisotropic diffusivity tensor read:

d_i ˆC_so = ∂_z γ [∂_x~ (κ_x~x~ ∂_x~ ˆC) + ∂_x~ (κ_x~y~ ∂_y~ ˆC) + ∂_y~ (κ_x~y~ ∂_x~ ˆC) + ∂_y~ (κ_y~y~ ∂_y~ ˆC)], (7)

This expression shows that the diffusivity is dependent on 3 scalars that measure both the intensity of the diffusivity and its orientation. Indeed, since the off-diagonal terms are strictly identical in (6), it simply induces a rotation of diffusivity, which will act independently along its two orthogonal natural directions (directions after rotation). Here, it becomes apparent that the use of a single coefficient cannot fully represent the complexity of these isopycnal transformations, both in terms of intensity and directionality.

Computation of epineutral flux
One last difficulty is to estimate the gradient along neutral density69 (or epineutral gradient) as expressed in (7): computing the ∇_n (or ∂_x~ and ∂_y~). As an example, but it would be equivalent for the meridional direction, for the zonal direction, we have:

∂_x~ σ ≈ ∂_x σ + s_x ∂_z σ, (8)

where σ is any scalar quantity (e.g., Temperature or Salinity), s_x = δz/Δx is the zonal component of the isopycnal slope, Δσ|γ,x,z is the difference in σ at constant γ, x, and z, respectively, Δx~ is the distance at constant γ along the zonal direction, and Δx and δz are the zonal and vertical distances, respectively, covered by the neutral density surface. In this calculation, a few approximations have been done: (i) Δx~ ≈ Δx^2 + δz^2, assuming that the epineutral displacement can be geometrically approximated by the zonal and vertical displacement; (ii) δz ≪ Δx, assuming that the vertical displacement of the epineutral is weak compared to the zonal one (i.e., small slope approximation65), allowing a Taylor expansion of the denominator; and (iii) ∂_x σ and ∂_z σ are constant over Δx and δz, respectively. Equivalently, we have ∂_y~ σ ≈ ∂_y σ + s_y ∂_z σ, where s_y is the meridional component of the isopycnal slope. Note that there exist more complex but more accurate computation methods of the neutral slopes and gradients, which are key when the slopes become important70,71. However, in our application, the slopes remain weak, with a maximum slope magnitude of 0.08 and a median value of 0.0001.

The slope is defined through the horizontal gradients of Absolute Salinity (S_A) and Conservative Temperature (Θ), by setting ∂_x~ γ = 0 and ∂_y~ γ = 0, such as:

s = - (α ∇_h Θ - β ∇_h S_A) / (∂_z γ), (9)

where ∇_h is the horizontal gradient, and α and β are the thermal expansion and haline contraction coefficients, respectively. s^2 is the magnitude of the slope measured through the components inner product (=s_x^2 + s_y^2).

This epineutral formulation for the gradients allows us to compute an approximation of the isopycnal diffusion, described in (5) and (7), for any tracer ˆC as a function of Cartesian coordinates. This reads:

d_i ˆC_so ≈ ∂_z γ [∂_x (κ_x~x~ (∂_x ˆC + s_x ∂_z ˆC)) + ∂_y (κ_x~y~ (∂_x ˆC + s_x ∂_z ˆC)) + ∂_x (κ_x~y~ (∂_y ˆC + s_y ∂_z ˆC)) + ∂_y (κ_y~y~ (∂_y ˆC + s_y ∂_z ˆC)) + s_x ∂_z (κ_x~x~ (∂_x ˆC + s_x ∂_z ˆC)) + s_x ∂_z (κ_x~y~ (∂_y ˆC + s_y ∂_z ˆC)) + s_y ∂_z (κ_x~y~ (∂_x ˆC + s_x ∂_z ˆC)) + s_y ∂_z (κ_y~y~ (∂_y ˆC + s_y ∂_z ˆC))], (10)

This is the formulation, which includes anisotropic, isopycnal diffusivities, that is used in our study.

Water mass transformation rates
Building on (10), the action of the isopycnal turbulent term could be further estimated in terms of transformation rates56,72 as:

Ψ_Θ = ∂_γ ∫Σ(γ0≤γ) α d_i Θ_so dΣ Δz, (11a)

Ψ_S_A = ∂_γ ∫Σ(γ0≤γ) β d_i S_A_so dΣ Δz, (11b)

where Σ(γ0≤γ) is the surface of a tracer class below the threshold value γ at 1000 m depth. Here Ψ_Θ and Ψ_S_A represent neutral density transformations through temperature or salinity changes over a layer of thickness Δz, respectively. These transformations are expressed in Sv, where 1 Sv ≡ 10^6 m^2 s^-1. In practice, the transformations are estimated using neutral density increment (we chose: Δγ = 0.03 kg m^-3). For consistency, the layer thickness can be estimated though the scaling: Δz ≈ Δγ (∂_z γ)^-1 (which derives from dγ = ∂_x γ dx + ∂_y γ dy + ∂_z γ dz). Computation over the globe at 1000 m depth show values from 10 m to more than 3000 m (Supplementary Fig. 1a). In particular, the thickness is significantly more important in the Southern Ocean (e.g., the Weddell Sea) and in the subpolar North Atlantic (e.g., Labrador Sea) than in the rest of the globe. However, extrapolating our computation over more than 3000 m is inconsistent with our knowledge of vertical variations of diffusivity coefficient: existence of a steering level40,41 and variations with Eddy Kinetic Energy36. Hence, we have chosen to restrict the layer thickness amplitude. We have used a uniform layer thickness based on the median value: Δz = 70 m (Supplementary Fig. 1b), regardless of the local stratification (∂_z γ). Hence, our results, despite being in Sverdrup, only reflect a slice of the ocean at 1000 m depth.

These transformations mathematically expressed a probability density function of density changes induced by cooling/warming or freshening/salinification per neutral density classes, respectively. They physically correspond to the volume of water at a given density that is gaining/loosing density by cooling/warming or by salinification/freshening, respectively.

These transformation rates (Ψ_Θ and Ψ_S_A) can be interpreted as the component of the total transformation induced by isopycnal turbulence. To summarize, (11) shows the existence of transformations when both isopycnal oceanic turbulence and isopycnal tracer gradients are present (Fig. 2). In this framework, one can compute transformations associated to temperature and salinity (Fig. 5). The sum of the two transformations with respect to neutral density classes can also be defined as: Ψ_Θ + Ψ_S_A. This sum is expected to be zero and, therefore, reflects the computation errors (Fig. 5e and f).

Tracer fields, diffusivity data, and computation method
One can compute a tracer transformation and transformation rates by knowing two properties:
1. ˆC and ∂_z ˆC (as well as ∂_z γ) at all locations [∀ (x, y)] along the depth, but primarily above the maximum Argo depth sampling of ~2000 m for robustness. In this study, C can be Conservative Temperature or Absolute Salinity (Fig. 1a, b);
2. K at all locations [∀ (x, y)] at the constant depth, which is determined by Argo deep displacements at their parking depth36 (Fig. 1d–f).

Hence, the main constraint occurs through K which is only determined at Argo float parking depth (mainly located at ~1000 m) and determines the focused depth of our study.

We have used the two-dimensional gridded direct estimate of the turbulent anisotropic, isopycnal diffusivity coefficients derived from Argo deep displacements36, which are available35 at https://doi.org/10.17882/91335, and the global three-dimensional ISAS17 gridded temperature and salinity data derived from objective analysis of in situ observations43 and available at https://doi.org/10.17882/52367. The diffusivity coefficients were obtained by reconstructing the turbulent field from deep Argo displacement. This reconstructed turbulent field was used to determine the local dispersion of a locally-injected spike of passive tracer, the rates of dispersion estimating the local diffusivity coefficients along the zonal, meridional, and cross directions. This allows for the full determination of the diffusivity tensor, rather than a single coefficient as often done33,34,39.

In practice, after conversion of the data to Conservative Temperature and Absolute Salinity, as well as the computation of neutral density, all the computations are done using 3°×3° cells (i.e., the native cell of the diffusivity coefficients) on 1°×1° grid (i.e., the native grid of the diffusivity coefficients). Data are vertically averaged over 40 m bins, and vertical levels (needed for the computation of vertical gradients) are separated by 20 m. All conversions to Conservative Temperature and Absolute Salinity, as well as computation of neutral density, are done using the Gibbs SeaWater Oceanographic Toolbox of TEOS-10 code.

For the water masses framework, we have identified six Water Masses located at the depth of the study49. They are defined through their temperature and salinity range. They are the Mediterranean Water (MW), the Red Sea–Persian Gulf Intermediate Water (RSPGIW), the Antarctic Intermediate Water (AAIW), the North Atlantic Water (NADW), the Circumpolar Deep Water (CDW), and the AntArctic Bottom Water (AABW).

Alternative Diffusivity Coefficients
To test the importance of using spatially-varying and anisotropic isopycnal diffusivity coefficients, we have tested a range of less complex diffusivity coefficients:
1. Spatially-uniform and isotropic isopycnal diffusivity coefficients: the diffusivity coefficients are set to κ_Uni&Iso_x~x~ = κ_Uni&Iso_y~y~ = (κ_x~x~ + κ_y~y~)/2 and κ_Uni&Iso_x~y~ = 0. These coefficients are applied to (5).
2. Spatially-varying and isotropic isopycnal diffusivity coefficients: the diffusivity coefficients are set to κ_Var&Iso_x~x~ = κ_Var&Iso_y~y~ = (κ_x~x~ + κ_y~y~)/2 and κ_Var&Iso_x~y~ = 0. These coefficients are applied to (5).

To compare transformations using the different versions of the diffusivity, we used a relative error (RE) using the most complete version as the reference. This reads:

RE = sign(log(Ψ_comp / Ψ_ref)) * |log(Ψ_comp / Ψ_ref)|, (12)

where Ψ_ref is the reference transformation (i.e., most complete diffusivity), Ψ_comp is the transformation used for comparison (i.e., less complete diffusivity), and the log term allow to estimate the sign of the mis-estimation (positive and negative for over- and under-estimation, respectively).

In addition to ensuring the robustness of our results, we have tested two other diffusivity coefficient datasets. They have been computed using different methods and/or different observations. Hence, we will also test a modified version of our dataset, which is more aligned with the constraints of these two datasets and allows a fairer comparison between the three datasets.

a. The first dataset will be named Groeskamp and corresponds to spatially-varying coefficients34. This dataset is available at: https://figshare.com/articles/dataset/Groeskamp_et_al_2020_-_mixing_diffusivities/12554555. The Groeskamp diffusivity coefficients (κ_Groeskamp) are obtained using a mixing length closure theory to extract cross-flow diffusivity coefficients from salinity ocean observations. These coefficients cover the full depth of the ocean but we extracted their values at 1000 m (Fig. 6a). Then, to be applied in our framework, we set this single spatially-varying coefficient as spatially-varying but isotropic coefficients: κ_Groeskamp_x~x~ = κ_Groeskamp_y~y~ = κ_Groeskamp and κ_Groeskamp_x~y~ = 0. Then we apply this set of coefficients to (5).

b. The second dataset will be named Roach and also correspond to spatially varying diffusivity coefficients39. This dataset is available at: https://github.com/croachutas/Isopycnal_Diffusivity. The Roach coefficients (κ_Roach) use a pairwise distance from deep Argo float displacements to infer the cross-flow diffusivity coefficients. By construction, this dataset is restricted to our 1000 m studied depth (Fig. 6b). As for the Groeskamp diffusivity coefficients, we set this single spatially varying coefficient as isotropic spatially varying coefficients: κ_Roach_x~x~ = κ_Roach_y~y~ = κ_Roach and κ_Roach_x~y~ = 0. This is applied to (5).

c. Since these two set of diffusion coefficients were computed as cross-flow diffusion coefficients, consistently, we have used our secondary diffusivity coefficient (κ_s) to have a fairer comparison with our diffusivity dataset39. The secondary diffusivity coefficient is the second eigenvalue of the diffusivity tensor (K) described in (6). It is, by construction, weaker than the primary eigenvalue and is more consistent with the cross-flow diffusivity coefficient (i.e., avoiding subgrid stirring and shearing). In principle, this secondary diffusivity is associated with a particular isopycnal direction (i.e., the second eigenvector of the diffusivity tensor). However, here for fair comparison with Groeskamp and Roach diffusivity coefficients described above, we have also applied it as a spatially varying and isotropic isopycnal diffusivity coefficient. Hence, it is set as: κ_Var&Isosec_x~x~ = κ_Var&Isosec_y~y~ = κ_s and κ_Var&Isosec_x~y~ = 0. These coefficients are applied to (5).

Finally, for comparison purposes, we have computed the diapycnal transformation as a vertical diffusion: d_i ˆC_ia = ∂_z (κ_z ∂_z ˆC), where κ_z is the vertical diffusivity coefficient. We have used spatially varying diffusivity coefficients59,60 available at https://doi.org/10.17882/73082, and have extracted the corresponding values for 1000 m depth (Supplementary Fig. 2). This shows the expected topographic control of the vertical diffusion coefficients.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
Summary
The authors apply a new estimate of epineutral mesoscale eddy diffusivities at 1000 dbar (based on statistics of Argo
parking drift; published separately) to a T&S climatology (previously published) to estimate isoneutral eddy-driven water
mass transformations in temperature and salinity coordinates. The key results are that (1) transformation rates are poorly
estimated if one uses a globally-constant isoneutral eddy diffusivity (as most climate models presently do) and (2) most of
this transformation occurs in Southern Ocean water masses, where both diffusivities and mean isoneutral property gradients
are large.
Major comments
I have some major concerns about (1) the methodology, (2) the contextualization in terms of the broader literature, and (3)
the clarity of communication of the results. The results are interesting but I think not as ground-breaking as the abstract
makes it sound. I would recommend a decision of Reject and Resubmit.
The main result is the calculation of water mass transformation rates (in temperature and salinity coordinates) due to
isoneutral eddy mixing. As the authors note several times, they are by observational constraints of the Argo parking depth
constrained to the 1000 dbar surface. What they do not sufficiently explain to the reader is that their choice of scaling these
point-wise transformation rates by a 100m layer is entirely arbitrary. In fact, it is not even really clear to me how the water
mass transformation calculations are made. Water masses transformations are inherently three dimensional processes that
the authors are approximating by a two dimensional slice and then scaling up arbitrarily. The description in lines 410-414
(plus equation 11) is confusing even to someone with a lot of experience thinking about water mass transformations, so I
suspect the general reader of Nature Comms will be lost. There are also some things I don’t understand about their results,
such as: on L. 164-166, it doesn’t look like these actually line up that well to me? Can you just convert these to both be in Sv
or Sv m-1 and add them together so we can see what the net transformation in density coordinates is? What does it mean
about your calculation if this is very different from zero?
The authors cite most (but not all) of the key references in the literature, but they never contextualize any of their results in
terms of these references. For instance, they mention early on that isopycnal transformations have previously mostly been
inferred indirectly using inverse models (I am thinking mostly of the Groeskamp papers), but they never circle back to discuss
how their results compare to these estimates! Are they very similar? Very different? Should we trust yours more, or theirs?
Do the differences tell us anything? Also, they claim to have “unveiled” these “hidden” isopycnal transformations, but they
are hardly the first to make estimates of these transformations–even if they may have a case for their estimate being the most
sophisticated since it uses independent datasets with a spatially-variable eddy diffusivity. I recommend referencing papers
that discuss the impact of isoneutral mixing in climate models (two recent examples:
https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1029/2019GL085208 and
https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1029/2021MS002914).
The roles of eddy-bolus velocities (or the skew-symmetric part of the diffusivity tensor) and the diapycnal velocity in the
ocean & climate system are unjustifiably downplayed to make their isoneutral mixing sound more important than it is. The
authors in some places forget the qualifier that they are only discussing the isopycnal mixing role of eddies and make
statements like “since eddies induce a flow along isopycnals, they cannot modify density… hence the circulation”, which are
not true if one always considers the leading-order quasi-advective role that eddies play in the general circulation. Also, the
comparison with diapycnal mixing transformations (19x smaller!) feels disingenuous; the reason people usually talk about
diapycnal mixing is not because how it transforms the temperature or salinity of water masses, but how it does so
diapycnally in a way that no other process in the ocean interior can.
Some of the key points are poorly articulated and difficult to decipher. In most cases I could eventually decipher what you are
trying to say, but not always (see minor comments).
Finally, the braggadocious tone of the writing is off-putting and I encourage the authors to tone it down. The entire
manuscript is written as though the authors are the first to realize that eddies are rapidly mixing temperature and salinity
along isopycnals, or at least the first to make an estimate of it. Some other examples: 1) Water mass transformation is a
framework that is more than 50 years old, so calling it “state-of-the-art” is a tough sell. 2) The other “state-of-the-art”
framework is the authors’ novel AI-based method for estimating turbulent anisotropic diffusivities. It is indeed very interesting
and–to my knowledge–a useful novel approach, but the authors don’t actually go any further in describing it in this
manuscript than stating its name (the “Analog method”) and citing their prior work! 3) Given how impactful this data set is in
this manuscript, it deserves at least a paragraph in the method section. (There is plenty of fluff in the introduction and
conclusions that you could cut out to make space).
Minor comments:
Eq. (4) – I understand where the authors are coming from, but it doesn’t really make sense to decompose the transformations
in this way because isopycnal + diapycnal already accounts for all directions. Either choose a two-way decomposition
(isopycnal vs. diapycnal) or explain that you are breaking these down by process: mixed-layer turbulence (strong in all
directions), interior mesoscale turbulence (isopycnal), and small-scale turbulence (in all three directions, but the isopycnal
component is swamped out by the mesoscale isopycnal so can be approximated by diapycnal).
Figure 3. Colormaps are not very interpretable and I think very bad for people with colorblindness.
Figure S1. Why not convert both to Sv so they can be directly compared? “For the isotropic diffusivity” I think should read
“For the anisotropic diffusivity”. Caption should clarify these are “Water mass transformations in density space” or something.
L. 374-375: I don’t understand this.
Why epineutral rather than isoneutral? Is epineutral more specifically a geometric descriptor?

Summary
The authors apply a new estimate of epineutral mesoscale eddy diffusivities at 1000 dbar
(based on statistics of Argo parking drift; published separately) to a T&S climatology

You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

The ocean, because of its ability to store heat and as the biggest mediator of water exchanges on Earth, modulates the climate from years to centuries. By combining Water Mass transformation and the Temporal-Residual-Mean frameworks, together with a direct estimation of turbulent diffusivity (computed through an artificial intelligence method), we determine temperature and salinity transformations along density surfaces. Because isopycnal transformations barely alter the density field, they remain hidden from the ocean dynamics. Here we unveil these hidden, isopycnal transformations from in situ observations at 1000-m depth. We show that these isopycnal transformations are 5 times as large as their diapycnal counterpart and are occurring for ~67% in the Southern Ocean. Our estimations stress the role of the spatially-varying and anisotropic characteristics of isopycnal diffusion, often not considered in ocean models. This has major consequences for our understanding of the role of the ocean in response to anthropogenic climate changes.

---

## Introduction

Ocean circulation transports a vast amount of water over the globe (up to 150 Sv, where 1 Sv ≡ 10^6 m^3 s^-1, in the Antarctic Circumpolar Current, for instance)1. This large-scale ocean circulation is also associated with transport of heat (up to 1.5 PW northward at 20°N)2 and freshwater (around 0.5 Sv southward at 35°N in the North Atlantic)3. The former is a fundamental component of the climate equilibrium and adjustment by transporting the excess of heat from the tropics to the poles. Whereas the latter indirectly reflects the geographical pattern of evaporation, precipitation, river discharge, and ice melting, all taking part in the water cycle. In particular, the ocean is the most important region of precipitation and evaporation (i.e., 75% and 85%, respectively), making it particularly relevant for the Earth water cycle4.

Beyond this equilibrated view, the Earth is experiencing changes since the pre-industrial era, with a significant amount of anthropogenically-induced greenhouse gazes released into the atmosphere5. As a consequence, the surface atmospheric temperature is increasing5, despite a significant mitigation by the ocean, with an ocean absorption of about 90% of the Earth’s heat excess5–7. Together with this warming, the water cycle is also affected8. These changes, either directly (when over the ocean) or indirectly through runoffs (when overland), are imprinted in the ocean freshwater transport9,10 through, for instance, modification of the ocean salinity distribution11. Hence, the ocean heat and freshwater transports are central actors of the Earth equilibrium and climate changes.

Mesoscale eddies are ubiquitous worldwide in the ocean12 and, unlike the mean transport, they contribute to the heat and freshwater transport in two-fold. Firstly, equivalently to the laminar component, they move ocean water properties (i.e., its temperature and salinity) in a conserving manner within the ocean. Secondly, eddies also induce a transformation of these properties through turbulent diffusion13 (e.g., mixing cold and warm waters or salty and fresh ones). Transformations of seawater properties can occur either through interactions with the atmosphere at the ocean surface or through turbulent diffusion in the ocean interior. Whereas the former is easier to estimate8,14, the latter has always been more difficult to assess and is often deduced using inverse methodology15–18. Assessing the role of turbulent eddy diffusion for heat and freshwater transports and for the transformation of seawater properties is a timely question of ocean and climate sciences, as demonstrated by numerous numerical model studies19–21.

There has been a large range of studies on Water Mass Transformations22–28. These studies often assess the transformations in terms of temperature and salinity changes, without specifically separating the respective role of isopycnal and diapycnal transformations. In parallel, the role of diapycnal diffusion on temperature and salinity transformations in the ocean interior has been well established16,29. More recently, studies have suggested the key role of isopycnal processes on heat and freshwater uptakes30,31, opening the possibility of an important role of the isopycnal diffusion. This has been further confirmed as potentially important in the North Atlantic for the maintenance of the mean temperature and salinity structure32. However, these studies rely on either numerical models or inverse methods, both intrinsically depending on a chosen closure scheme (and sometimes imposed parameters). Hence, it is key to use direct observations to assess whether isopycnal or diapycnal diffusion is dominant in the ocean interior. Indeed, in ocean science, where reproducible controlled experiments are not possible, the use of direct observations is the only way to validate or invalidate hypotheses derived from these numerical or inverse modeling approaches.

In this work, we use direct observations to assess the changes and transformations of temperature and salinity induced by mesoscale eddy turbulence, which acts as an equivalent isopycnal turbulent diffusion. We show that, at 1000 m depth, these temperature and salinity changes mainly occurred in the Southern Ocean and along the Gulf Stream. These isopycnal changes induce temperature and salinity transformations significantly more important than their diapycnal equivalents. We also conclude that the spatially variable and anisotropic nature of the isopycnal turbulent diffusion is keys for an accurate estimation of the temperature and salinity transformations.

---

## Results

The major difficulty of obtaining robust, direct estimations of heat and freshwater transformations by eddies comes from the need of knowing turbulent diffusive coefficients independently of temperature and salinity fields (to avoid the dependence of the results to a closure scheme)33,34. Here, to circumvent this difficulty, we have used the recently estimated diffusivity coefficients35 derived from Argo float deep displacements36. This dataset has been obtained using a class of data-driven Artificial Intelligence methods: the Analog Method37,38. There, the spatially varying and anisotropic diffusivity coefficients were estimated through local tracer dispersion induced by a turbulent velocity field reconstructed from deep Argo displacements. This dataset provides the full diffusivity tensor, explicitly acknowledging the anisotropy, rather than a single diffusivity coefficient, as most commonly done33,34,39. These resulting diffusivity coefficients are strong where the flow is strong (Fig. 1d, e), but with a slight spatial offset with the core of the currents40,41, hence with the largest density gradients. This could be rationalized by the existence of Kinetic Energy transfers42. These coefficients (Fig. 1d, e) together with temperature and salinity fields from gridded ISAS17 product43 (Optimal Interpolation44 from Argo profiles, Fig. 1a, b) allow us to have a direct estimation of isopycnal heat and freshwater transformations and uncover an unobserved facet of deep ocean circulation.

Effect of isopycnal turbulent diffusion
In the present study, we assess the global effect of the turbulent diffusion on temperature and salinity fields. However, because of observational constraints (i.e., the typical parking depth of Argo float deep displacements), our study focuses at 1000 m depth. This depth is particularly relevant for estimating heat and freshwater transports and seawater property transformations for two reasons. (1) It is close to the depth of the maximum of the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (depth of no-motion for this circulation, as estimated at 26.5°N in the North Atlantic by RAPID)45. (2) It is the depth with the largest contrast in salinity46,47, but also includes signatures of the coldest waters47 (Fig. 1).

The transformation of seawater properties works hand in hand with the concept of Water Masses48. Water Masses are volumes of water with consistent seawater properties (Fig. 1f) that are set through ocean-atmosphere exchange at the ocean surface, where water masses originate. They then spread within the ocean through advection and mixing and are transformed by the latter. At 1000 m depth, we will consider three intermediate water masses: Red Sea–Persian Gulf Intermediate Water (RSPGIW) formed in the Red Sea and Persian Gulf49, the Mediterranean Water50 (MW) reaching the Atlantic through the Strait of Gibraltar, and the AntArctic Intermediate Water51 (AAIW) intersecting the 1000-m depth along the Polar Front52. We will also consider more dense Water Masses, namely the North Atlantic Deep Water (NADW), its transformed southern extension, the Circumpolar Deep Water53 (CDW), and the Antarctic Bottom Water54 (AABW). Despite not being their depth of maximum intrusion, these Water Masses are present at 1000 m depth in the high latitudes of the North Atlantic and of the Southern Ocean (Fig. 1f).

To estimate the impact of the turbulent diffusion on the temperature and salinity of these water masses, we follow the Temporal-Residual-Mean framework (see Methods – Isopycnal Turbulent Transformation Framework)13. This framework disentangles advective and mixing effects when eddy turbulence is averaged. This allows for an accurate attribution of eddy-induced transport and transformation. Also, this framework acknowledges that transformations act within isopycnal layers as epineutral flux (Fig. 2). To this purpose averaging are done along-isopycnal, so that fictitious diapycnal transport, due to incorrect estimates of the isopycnal slopes, can be limited55. This transformation-induced process has almost no signature on the density field (except for the weak cabbeling and thermobaricity components, although they remain crucial for the density transformations56), nor pressure, nor circulation. As a consequence, there is no impact on Potential Energy, and it can act passively, as long as Eddy Kinetic Energy remains to maintain the turbulent diffusion. In this sense, for the ocean dynamics, it remains hidden along the isopycnals (Fig. 1c). However, it still contributes to heat and freshwater transports from cold to warm and from salty to fresh regions, respectively. This process can be described in the form of temperature and salinity rates of change or of water-mass transformation rates (see Methods – Water Mass Transformation Rates). The rates of change of a material property (temperature or salinity) measure the amount of warming/cooling or salinification/freshening induced by the isopycnal turbulent diffusion; whereas the transformation accounts for the amount of seawater that have their properties transformed by this process.

Rates of temperature and salinity change
As mentioned above, the isopycnal diffusion of temperature and salinity can be assessed as the induced rates of change in terms of temperature and salinity [see Methods – (10)]. High magnitudes of the rates of change are due to high diffusivity coefficients, sharp isopycnal temperature or salinity gradients, or a combination of both. At 1000 m depth, we find that they are of the order of kelvins per year or tenth of (g kg^-1) per year [or a few 10^-8 K s^-1 and 10^-9 g kg^-1 s^-1] for temperature and salinity, respectively. These rates of change are mainly located in the Southern Ocean, along the Antarctic Circumpolar Current, and, to a lesser extent, in the North West of the North Atlantic (Figs. 3a and 4a). Indeed, the Southern Ocean accounts for 67% of the global rates of change for temperature and salinity [as measured by the R^2 of the transformations described in (11)], despite representing only 31% of the global ocean area. When including the North Atlantic it reaches 95% for temperature and salinity rates of change. A local maximum of these rates of change can be seen in the Zapiola gyre, which corresponds to a local maximum of diffusivity coefficients (Fig. 1d, e). There is also significant rates of change along the Agulhas return current and its merging with the Antarctic Circumpolar Current, which also corresponds to a local maximum of diffusivity coefficients. Indeed, between South Africa and the Kerguelen plateau, there is a warming and salinification of the relatively cold and salty AAIW (Figs. 3a and 4a), a cooling and freshening of the relatively warm and fresh AAIW, and a warming and salinification of the warm and salty residual of RSGPIW (trapped in the Agulhas system57, Fig. 1b).

Unlike the geographical map that reveals where the rates of change are located, the TS-diagram (i.e., representation with temperature-salinity axes) reveals which water masses are subjected to the isopycnal diffusion (i.e., change along isopycnals). This can be represented globally (insets in Figs. 3a and 4a) or displayed for each relevant basin (following the division of Fig. 1f), which allows a simpler relation with local Water Masses (Fig. 3b–e and 4b–e). In the North Atlantic, despite the weak isopycnal turbulent diffusion coefficients in the subtropical gyre interior (Fig. 1d, e), temperature and salinity rates of change within the MW (along the 27.6-27.8 kg m^-3 density class) are visible with a slight cooling and a freshening of MW (Fig. 3b). A more important cooling and freshening is also visible at the edge between MW and NADW. In the Southern Ocean, the geographical separation is quite revealing. It suggests different water masses at play for each of the three sectors (Atlantic, Indian, and Pacific). In the Atlantic sector of the Southern Ocean, we observe a cooling and freshening of CDW and a warming and salinification of AAIW and AABW (Figs. 3c and 4c). In the Indian and Pacific sectors, the rates of change correspond to a warming and salinification of the AABW, a cooling and freshening of the CDW, a warming and salinification of the coldest and freshest portion of the AAIW, and a cooling and freshening of the warmest and saltiest portion of the AAIW (Figs. 3d, e and 4d, e). In the Indian sector, there is also a warming and salinification of the warmer portion of the AAIW, which derives from RSPGIW57.

To further quantify these effects, the isopycnal turbulent diffusion can also be expressed as Water Masses Transformation (see Methods – Water Mass Transformation Rates). As discussed earlier, since the isopycnal temperature and salinity gradients are important given the range of different Water Masses. At 25°W we have: AntArctic Bottom Water (AABW), AntArctic Intermediate Water (AAIW), Mediterranean Water (MW), North Atlantic Deep Water (NADW), and Circumpolar Deep Water (CDW). As suggested by the schematic (a and b), it is possible to compute the rates of change, following (10), and the corresponding water mass transformation, following (11), associated to a tracer (e.g., temperature or salinity).

## Methods

Isopycnal turbulent transformation framework
Starting from the advection equation for a tracer (which could be temperature or salinity) away from forcing (mainly occurring at the ocean surface) and for high Péclet number (Pe ≫ 1, measuring the advection to diffusion ratio), we have:

D_t C = 0, (1)

where C is the tracer concentration and D_t is the material derivative (=∂_t + u∂_x + v∂_y + w∂_z, where t is time, x, y, and z are the zonal, meridional, and vertical coordinates, and u, v, and w are the zonal, meridional, and vertical velocities).

This equation can be modified to show the evolution of the large-spatial scale or long-timescale by splitting each term in an Eulerian mean (¯) and its associated anomaly ('). This reads:

D_t ¯C = -∂_x ¯(u'C') - ∂_y ¯(v'C') - ∂_z ¯(w'C'), (2)

where D_t is the mean material derivative (=∂_t + ¯u∂_x + ¯v∂_y + ¯w∂_z). This shows that several mean (¯C, ¯u, ¯v, and ¯w) and turbulent (¯(u'C'), ¯(v'C'), and ¯(w'C')) terms contribute to the maintenance of the mean state.

In the Temporal-Residual-Mean framework, we can redistribute the terms13,64 so that the evolution of the mean tracer is:

D_b_t ˆC = d ˆC, (3)

where ˆC is the modified tracer, D_b_t is the modified material derivative [=∂_t + ˆu∂_x + ˆv∂_y + ˆw∂_z, and ˆu=¯u+˜u, ˆv=¯v+˜v, and ˆw=¯w+˜w, where ˜u, ˜v, and ˜w are the zonal, meridional, and vertical eddy-induced velocities, respectively], and d ˆC is the transformation term. This expression suggests that the modified tracer is advected by both the mean and the eddy-induced velocity65 and transformed. In this Temporal-Residual-Mean framework, the eddy-induced advection and the transformation are consequences of the skew-symmetric and symmetric components of the turbulent flux, respectively. This framework is particularly useful to accurately separate and attribute the advection and mixing effects of averaged eddy turbulence. The advection effect only displaces tracer properties, whereas the mixing effect changes tracer properties. Hence, this framework avoids the misinterpretation of eddy-induced transport by horizontal turbulence as a transformation.

In the ocean interior (i.e., below mixed layer depth), we have neglected the potential effect of horizontal transformation (important within the mixed layer). In the rest of the study, we will focus on the isopycnal component of these fluxes and compare it to the diapycnal one. Note that isopycnal heat and freshwater transformations act along a constant density surface, thus, by construction, they avoid density gradients. Although the diapycnal component, induced by small-scale mixing processes66, will be used as a reference. It is worth noting that the use horizontal diffusion instead of isopycnal diffusion outside of the mixed layer is fundamentally flawed55. With this approximation, we would find transformations that are completely missing the correct warming/cooling and freshening/salinification. Also, as expected for such flawed approximation, the compensation between temperature and salinity changes are missed. This would result in unrealistic transformations.

Following a downgradient flux closure13,67 (i.e., Fick’s law), the density-weighted isopycnal transformation reads:

d_i ˆC_so = ∂_z γ ∇_n · K · ∇_n (∂_z γ)^-1, (5)

where ∇_n refers to the gradient along the neutral density (γ) and K is the spatially-varying and anisotropic isopycnal diffusivity tensor. Here, the gradient is computed using the projected nonorthogonal approach68,69. The diffusivity tensor is expressed as:

K = [κ_x~x~ κ_x~y~; κ_x~y~ κ_y~y~], (6)

where x~ and y~ are the zonal and meridional direction along neutral density, respectively, and κ_x~x~, κ_y~y~, and κ_x~y~ are the zonal, meridional, and cross diffusivities along the neutral density, respectively. Hence, the isopycnal transformations for a spatially varying and anisotropic diffusivity tensor read:

d_i ˆC_so = ∂_z γ [∂_x~ (κ_x~x~ ∂_x~ ˆC) + ∂_x~ (κ_x~y~ ∂_y~ ˆC) + ∂_y~ (κ_x~y~ ∂_x~ ˆC) + ∂_y~ (κ_y~y~ ∂_y~ ˆC)], (7)

This expression shows that the diffusivity is dependent on 3 scalars that measure both the intensity of the diffusivity and its orientation. Indeed, since the off-diagonal terms are strictly identical in (6), it simply induces a rotation of diffusivity, which will act independently along its two orthogonal natural directions (directions after rotation). Here, it becomes apparent that the use of a single coefficient cannot fully represent the complexity of these isopycnal transformations, both in terms of intensity and directionality.

Computation of epineutral flux
One last difficulty is to estimate the gradient along neutral density69 (or epineutral gradient) as expressed in (7): computing the ∇_n (or ∂_x~ and ∂_y~). As an example, but it would be equivalent for the meridional direction, for the zonal direction, we have:

∂_x~ σ ≈ ∂_x σ + s_x ∂_z σ, (8)

where σ is any scalar quantity (e.g., Temperature or Salinity), s_x = δz/Δx is the zonal component of the isopycnal slope, Δσ|γ,x,z is the difference in σ at constant γ, x, and z, respectively, Δx~ is the distance at constant γ along the zonal direction, and Δx and δz are the zonal and vertical distances, respectively, covered by the neutral density surface. In this calculation, a few approximations have been done: (i) Δx~ ≈ Δx^2 + δz^2, assuming that the epineutral displacement can be geometrically approximated by the zonal and vertical displacement; (ii) δz ≪ Δx, assuming that the vertical displacement of the epineutral is weak compared to the zonal one (i.e., small slope approximation65), allowing a Taylor expansion of the denominator; and (iii) ∂_x σ and ∂_z σ are constant over Δx and δz, respectively. Equivalently, we have ∂_y~ σ ≈ ∂_y σ + s_y ∂_z σ, where s_y is the meridional component of the isopycnal slope. Note that there exist more complex but more accurate computation methods of the neutral slopes and gradients, which are key when the slopes become important70,71. However, in our application, the slopes remain weak, with a maximum slope magnitude of 0.08 and a median value of 0.0001.

The slope is defined through the horizontal gradients of Absolute Salinity (S_A) and Conservative Temperature (Θ), by setting ∂_x~ γ = 0 and ∂_y~ γ = 0, such as:

s = - (α ∇_h Θ - β ∇_h S_A) / (∂_z γ), (9)

where ∇_h is the horizontal gradient, and α and β are the thermal expansion and haline contraction coefficients, respectively. s^2 is the magnitude of the slope measured through the components inner product (=s_x^2 + s_y^2).

This epineutral formulation for the gradients allows us to compute an approximation of the isopycnal diffusion, described in (5) and (7), for any tracer ˆC as a function of Cartesian coordinates. This reads:

d_i ˆC_so ≈ ∂_z γ [∂_x (κ_x~x~ (∂_x ˆC + s_x ∂_z ˆC)) + ∂_y (κ_x~y~ (∂_x ˆC + s_x ∂_z ˆC)) + ∂_x (κ_x~y~ (∂_y ˆC + s_y ∂_z ˆC)) + ∂_y (κ_y~y~ (∂_y ˆC + s_y ∂_z ˆC)) + s_x ∂_z (κ_x~x~ (∂_x ˆC + s_x ∂_z ˆC)) + s_x ∂_z (κ_x~y~ (∂_y ˆC + s_y ∂_z ˆC)) + s_y ∂_z (κ_x~y~ (∂_x ˆC + s_x ∂_z ˆC)) + s_y ∂_z (κ_y~y~ (∂_y ˆC + s_y ∂_z ˆC))], (10)

This is the formulation, which includes anisotropic, isopycnal diffusivities, that is used in our study.

Water mass transformation rates
Building on (10), the action of the isopycnal turbulent term could be further estimated in terms of transformation rates56,72 as:

Ψ_Θ = ∂_γ ∫Σ(γ0≤γ) α d_i Θ_so dΣ Δz, (11a)

Ψ_S_A = ∂_γ ∫Σ(γ0≤γ) β d_i S_A_so dΣ Δz, (11b)

where Σ(γ0≤γ) is the surface of a tracer class below the threshold value γ at 1000 m depth. Here Ψ_Θ and Ψ_S_A represent neutral density transformations through temperature or salinity changes over a layer of thickness Δz, respectively. These transformations are expressed in Sv, where 1 Sv ≡ 10^6 m^2 s^-1. In practice, the transformations are estimated using neutral density increment (we chose: Δγ = 0.03 kg m^-3). For consistency, the layer thickness can be estimated though the scaling: Δz ≈ Δγ (∂_z γ)^-1 (which derives from dγ = ∂_x γ dx + ∂_y γ dy + ∂_z γ dz). Computation over the globe at 1000 m depth show values from 10 m to more than 3000 m (Supplementary Fig. 1a). In particular, the thickness is significantly more important in the Southern Ocean (e.g., the Weddell Sea) and in the subpolar North Atlantic (e.g., Labrador Sea) than in the rest of the globe. However, extrapolating our computation over more than 3000 m is inconsistent with our knowledge of vertical variations of diffusivity coefficient: existence of a steering level40,41 and variations with Eddy Kinetic Energy36. Hence, we have chosen to restrict the layer thickness amplitude. We have used a uniform layer thickness based on the median value: Δz = 70 m (Supplementary Fig. 1b), regardless of the local stratification (∂_z γ). Hence, our results, despite being in Sverdrup, only reflect a slice of the ocean at 1000 m depth.

These transformations mathematically expressed a probability density function of density changes induced by cooling/warming or freshening/salinification per neutral density classes, respectively. They physically correspond to the volume of water at a given density that is gaining/loosing density by cooling/warming or by salinification/freshening, respectively.

These transformation rates (Ψ_Θ and Ψ_S_A) can be interpreted as the component of the total transformation induced by isopycnal turbulence. To summarize, (11) shows the existence of transformations when both isopycnal oceanic turbulence and isopycnal tracer gradients are present (Fig. 2). In this framework, one can compute transformations associated to temperature and salinity (Fig. 5). The sum of the two transformations with respect to neutral density classes can also be defined as: Ψ_Θ + Ψ_S_A. This sum is expected to be zero and, therefore, reflects the computation errors (Fig. 5e and f).

Tracer fields, diffusivity data, and computation method
One can compute a tracer transformation and transformation rates by knowing two properties:
1. ˆC and ∂_z ˆC (as well as ∂_z γ) at all locations [∀ (x, y)] along the depth, but primarily above the maximum Argo depth sampling of ~2000 m for robustness. In this study, C can be Conservative Temperature or Absolute Salinity (Fig. 1a, b);
2. K at all locations [∀ (x, y)] at the constant depth, which is determined by Argo deep displacements at their parking depth36 (Fig. 1d–f).

Hence, the main constraint occurs through K which is only determined at Argo float parking depth (mainly located at ~1000 m) and determines the focused depth of our study.

We have used the two-dimensional gridded direct estimate of the turbulent anisotropic, isopycnal diffusivity coefficients derived from Argo deep displacements36, which are available35 at https://doi.org/10.17882/91335, and the global three-dimensional ISAS17 gridded temperature and salinity data derived from objective analysis of in situ observations43 and available at https://doi.org/10.17882/52367. The diffusivity coefficients were obtained by reconstructing the turbulent field from deep Argo displacement. This reconstructed turbulent field was used to determine the local dispersion of a locally-injected spike of passive tracer, the rates of dispersion estimating the local diffusivity coefficients along the zonal, meridional, and cross directions. This allows for the full determination of the diffusivity tensor, rather than a single coefficient as often done33,34,39.

In practice, after conversion of the data to Conservative Temperature and Absolute Salinity, as well as the computation of neutral density, all the computations are done using 3°×3° cells (i.e., the native cell of the diffusivity coefficients) on 1°×1° grid (i.e., the native grid of the diffusivity coefficients). Data are vertically averaged over 40 m bins, and vertical levels (needed for the computation of vertical gradients) are separated by 20 m. All conversions to Conservative Temperature and Absolute Salinity, as well as computation of neutral density, are done using the Gibbs SeaWater Oceanographic Toolbox of TEOS-10 code.

For the water masses framework, we have identified six Water Masses located at the depth of the study49. They are defined through their temperature and salinity range. They are the Mediterranean Water (MW), the Red Sea–Persian Gulf Intermediate Water (RSPGIW), the Antarctic Intermediate Water (AAIW), the North Atlantic Water (NADW), the Circumpolar Deep Water (CDW), and the AntArctic Bottom Water (AABW).

Alternative Diffusivity Coefficients
To test the importance of using spatially-varying and anisotropic isopycnal diffusivity coefficients, we have tested a range of less complex diffusivity coefficients:
1. Spatially-uniform and isotropic isopycnal diffusivity coefficients: the diffusivity coefficients are set to κ_Uni&Iso_x~x~ = κ_Uni&Iso_y~y~ = (κ_x~x~ + κ_y~y~)/2 and κ_Uni&Iso_x~y~ = 0. These coefficients are applied to (5).
2. Spatially-varying and isotropic isopycnal diffusivity coefficients: the diffusivity coefficients are set to κ_Var&Iso_x~x~ = κ_Var&Iso_y~y~ = (κ_x~x~ + κ_y~y~)/2 and κ_Var&Iso_x~y~ = 0. These coefficients are applied to (5).

To compare transformations using the different versions of the diffusivity, we used a relative error (RE) using the most complete version as the reference. This reads:

RE = sign(log(Ψ_comp / Ψ_ref)) * |log(Ψ_comp / Ψ_ref)|, (12)

where Ψ_ref is the reference transformation (i.e., most complete diffusivity), Ψ_comp is the transformation used for comparison (i.e., less complete diffusivity), and the log term allow to estimate the sign of the mis-estimation (positive and negative for over- and under-estimation, respectively).

In addition to ensuring the robustness of our results, we have tested two other diffusivity coefficient datasets. They have been computed using different methods and/or different observations. Hence, we will also test a modified version of our dataset, which is more aligned with the constraints of these two datasets and allows a fairer comparison between the three datasets.

a. The first dataset will be named Groeskamp and corresponds to spatially-varying coefficients34. This dataset is available at: https://figshare.com/articles/dataset/Groeskamp_et_al_2020_-_mixing_diffusivities/12554555. The Groeskamp diffusivity coefficients (κ_Groeskamp) are obtained using a mixing length closure theory to extract cross-flow diffusivity coefficients from salinity ocean observations. These coefficients cover the full depth of the ocean but we extracted their values at 1000 m (Fig. 6a). Then, to be applied in our framework, we set this single spatially-varying coefficient as spatially-varying but isotropic coefficients: κ_Groeskamp_x~x~ = κ_Groeskamp_y~y~ = κ_Groeskamp and κ_Groeskamp_x~y~ = 0. Then we apply this set of coefficients to (5).

b. The second dataset will be named Roach and also correspond to spatially varying diffusivity coefficients39. This dataset is available at: https://github.com/croachutas/Isopycnal_Diffusivity. The Roach coefficients (κ_Roach) use a pairwise distance from deep Argo float displacements to infer the cross-flow diffusivity coefficients. By construction, this dataset is restricted to our 1000 m studied depth (Fig. 6b). As for the Groeskamp diffusivity coefficients, we set this single spatially varying coefficient as isotropic spatially varying coefficients: κ_Roach_x~x~ = κ_Roach_y~y~ = κ_Roach and κ_Roach_x~y~ = 0. This is applied to (5).

c. Since these two set of diffusion coefficients were computed as cross-flow diffusion coefficients, consistently, we have used our secondary diffusivity coefficient (κ_s) to have a fairer comparison with our diffusivity dataset39. The secondary diffusivity coefficient is the second eigenvalue of the diffusivity tensor (K) described in (6). It is, by construction, weaker than the primary eigenvalue and is more consistent with the cross-flow diffusivity coefficient (i.e., avoiding subgrid stirring and shearing). In principle, this secondary diffusivity is associated with a particular isopycnal direction (i.e., the second eigenvector of the diffusivity tensor). However, here for fair comparison with Groeskamp and Roach diffusivity coefficients described above, we have also applied it as a spatially varying and isotropic isopycnal diffusivity coefficient. Hence, it is set as: κ_Var&Isosec_x~x~ = κ_Var&Isosec_y~y~ = κ_s and κ_Var&Isosec_x~y~ = 0. These coefficients are applied to (5).

Finally, for comparison purposes, we have computed the diapycnal transformation as a vertical diffusion: d_i ˆC_ia = ∂_z (κ_z ∂_z ˆC), where κ_z is the vertical diffusivity coefficient. We have used spatially varying diffusivity coefficients59,60 available at https://doi.org/10.17882/73082, and have extracted the corresponding values for 1000 m depth (Supplementary Fig. 2). This shows the expected topographic control of the vertical diffusion coefficients.
